current_status.before: Rescinded by court order as of 2026-09-23. Imperial County Superior Court Judge Jeffrey B. Jones entered judgment 2026-09-04 in favor of developer Imperial Valley Computer Manufacturing, LLC, finding neither Ordinance 1616 (the original moratorium) nor Ordinance 1618 (its ~10-month-15-day extension) made the causal finding of a 'current and immediate threat to public health, safety, or welfare' required by Gov. Code section 65858. A peremptory writ of mandate issued 2026-09-11 directs the County and Board of Supervisors to set aside both ordinances and stop using them to withhold, suspend, or refuse data-center permits. The County has said (per KYMA, 2026-09-22) it is working on a new moratorium addressing the court's concerns; no replacement had been adopted as of 2026-09-23. The Data Center Advisory Committee, created alongside the moratorium, continues to meet (inaugural meeting 2026-09-17) and is unaffected by the ruling. Separately, a different judge (L. Brooks Anderholt) has ordered a full CEQA environmental review of the underlying data center project in a related case, so the project itself remains stalled notwithstanding the moratorium's invalidation.
current_status.after: Ordinances 1616 and 1618 were repealed and set aside by the Board on October 6, 2026 in compliance with the court writ; the county said the urgency repeal took effect immediately. A separate October 6 moratorium was reported in local news; its later status was not verified.

outcome.before: Moratorium (Ordinances 1616 and 1618) adopted and extended to run through mid-2027, then invalidated by the Imperial County Superior Court (Judge Jeffrey B. Jones) in Imperial Valley Computer Manufacturing, LLC v. County of Imperial: judgment entered 2026-09-04, peremptory writ of mandate issued 2026-09-11 ordering the County to set aside and cease enforcing both ordinances because their findings did not satisfy Gov. Code section 65858's 'current and immediate threat' standard. current_status.before: Still in effect as of 2026-09-23, event-based: the July 21 second reading never occurred as planned. Court Chair Voegele ruled the Fiscal Court's 2026-08-24 special-called meeting void because the court failed to approve its own agenda, so the item restarted. On 2026-09-01 the Fiscal Court reconsidered and unanimously adopted substantive revisions to the draft regulations (still numbered KOC 26-920-5): striking all references to 'large'/'hyperscale' data centers while adding a 10 MW maximum power-capacity cap (effectively banning hyperscale projects), raising the square-footage cap for 'medium' data centers to 110,000 sq ft, and requiring two weeks' advance notice to property owners within 1,000 ft of a proposed site's neighborhood meeting. County Attorney D. Berry Baxter, backed by outside zoning counsel and the Kentucky Association of Counties, concluded KRS 100.211(8)'s 90-day deadline for zoning MAP amendments does not apply to this zoning TEXT amendment, so no statutory deadline forces a vote. The Fiscal Court's public hearing and final (second-reading) vote on KOC 26-920-5 is now calendared for 2026-10-06, after this research date. The moratorium (KOC 25-910-508, extended by KOC 25-910-520 'until data center regulations are approved') has no fixed end date -- it remains the operative instrument until that vote occurs (or another statutory event ends it), consistent with an Aug. 19, 2026 news report confirming the moratorium 'remains in place' pending the Fiscal Court's next action.

legal_basis.before: Seattle Ordinance No. 127447 (Council Bill 121214, amended), with companion Resolution 32204 (amended); adopted under the RCW 36.70A.390 interim-zoning-control procedure. Amends SMC 23.84A.008 to define "data center" as a facility used primarily for storing and processing digital data, with power capacity over 20 Megavolt-Amperes and requiring uninterruptible power, and imposes a moratorium on the filing, acceptance, processing, or approval of applications to establish or expand such uses.
legal_basis.after: Seattle Ordinance 127447 (Council Bill 121214), Sections 2-3: citywide moratorium on filing, acceptance, processing or approval of applications to establish, expand or change use to data centers, as principal or accessory uses. Definition requires primary use for computer/network equipment and digital-data functions, capacity above 20 MVA and generally uninterruptible power supplies with associated infrastructure. Section 2 exempts expansions of no more than an additional 20 MVA at facilities operating on the effective date that meet the definition or would meet it except for existing capacity at or below 20 MVA. Section 6 adopts Attachment A work plan under RCW 36.70A.390.

outcome.before: Moratorium enacted 2026-06-09; the city is using the pause and the companion Resolution 32204 working-group process to study grid, water, ratepayer, and environmental-justice impacts and to develop permanent siting/zoning rules, with reports and proposed permanent legislation due by January 2027.

key_provisions.before: Amends Ala. Code Sections 40-9B-3, 40-9B-4, 40-9B-4.1, and 40-23-35. Limits data processing center abatement periods beginning 2027-01-01, generally to 20 years, with added 10-year extension paths for certain investments. Requires certain 100 MW-plus data processing centers to pay state noneducational ad valorem taxes and sales/use tax on specified construction, power, backup generation, and battery purchases beginning 2027-01-01, subject to targeted-county gubernatorial authority. Extends the data processing center abatement sunset.
key_provisions.after: Amends Alabama data-processing-center tax abatements and sales-tax distribution. For qualifying abatements granted on or after January 1, 2027, revised duration tiers generally permit up to 20 years, with a conditional additional 10 years for qualified local investments. For centers with at least 100 MW peak demand, specified state noneducational ad valorem and construction-related transaction tax abatements generally end when property is placed in service, subject to eligible equipment and targeted-county gubernatorial exceptions. Extends the incentive application sunset and excludes specified incentives in projects executed before the effective date and expansions of those projects during the following ten years from the amendments to Sections 40-9B-3, 40-9B-4 and 40-9B-4.1. Act effective June 1, 2026.

Section 945.3 applies to data centers entering new transmission-level retail service interconnection agreements on or after 2027-01-01; demand response participation is optional.

key_provisions.before: Adds Idaho Code 61-335, titled 'New Large Load and Ratepayer Protection.' Defines a 'new large load' as a service-entrance load increase of 50 MW or more within a rolling 60-month period under a contract entered on or after 2026-07-01 (squarely covers data centers). Requires a PUC-approved service contract before a utility may serve such a load, including a commission 'no harm test'; makes the new large load responsible for its full cost of service (generation, transmission, substation, distribution); bars load-splitting to evade the threshold; requires financial security against stranded costs; and directs the commission to review rates in each general rate case to keep other ratepayers' bills from rising because of the new load.
key_provisions.after: Idaho Code 61-335 establishes a new large-load utility framework: a service entrance must have an increase in cumulative power requirement of at least 50 MW in any consecutive 60-month period and a public-utility contract entered on or after July 1, 2026. The increase is maximum contracted demand relative to the entrance’s highest contracted demand in the previous 60 months. The law requires commission-approved contracts and a no-harm test, full cost assignment, anti-evasion measures, financial security and rate-case review; data centers qualify only when the statutory criteria are met.

The retained comparison does not determine whether similar rules became law elsewhere.

Local-government permissions are excluded.

Chapter 4941 covers primarily or exclusively digital-information uses, including virtual-currency mining, on single or contiguous/adjacent/aggregated parcels, with peak demand greater than 25 MW at a single building or physical location; specified supply requirements concern new centers with aggregate monthly maximum demand greater than 250 MW. Sections 4941.02-.04 have exceptions for qualifying pre-effective-date utility contracts, subject to a commission-determined material-capacity-increase rule, and specified treatment for contracts under previously approved data-center tariffs.

key_provisions.before: Directs the Center for Local Government Services to provide data center ordinance assistance and model municipal standards.
key_provisions.after: House-amended PN 3174 proposes that the Local Government Commission develop and publish a model data-center zoning ordinance and provide municipal technical assistance, stakeholder consultation, annual updates and public comment. The print replaces the Center for Local Government Services as the responsible body; this is a proposal, not an enacted statewide zoning mandate.

key_provisions.before: Amends Right-to-Know Law to prohibit nondisclosure agreements concerning data center construction, development, or location.
key_provisions.after: House-amended PN 3724 proposes computer-data-center incentive certification and retention conditions: a community-protection plan, project-footprint reporting and specified NDA certification. The plan and NDA conditions exclude centers below 10 MW peak demand. Separate exceptions concern specified pre-construction engagement requirements where construction began earlier, and NDA certification for previously certified owners/operators or qualified tenants. This is not a general amendment banning every data-center NDA under the Right-to-Know Law.

end_condition.after: If enacted and a municipality adopts a pause, it may last no more than 180 days, retroactive to the specified public notice; the same procedure may not be used again for 18 months after formal expiration or repeal.

key_provisions.before: Amends the Municipalities Planning Code to allow a municipality to impose a 180-day pause on considering new data center development applications while it establishes or revises zoning ordinances for such facilities; applications filed during the pause are deemed received once the pause ends. Appears to be the bill introduced from the 'Proposed Zoning Consideration Period' co-sponsorship memo (#48467).
key_provisions.after: Senate-amended PN 3727 would let a municipality adopt a public-meeting resolution pausing acceptance of new data-center land-development applications for up to 180 days, retroactive to specified public notice. Earlier applications are exempt and continue under the applicable earlier rules; submissions during a pause are deemed received the following day after it ends. Repeat use is barred for 18 months following formal expiration or repeal. This is optional local authority, not a statewide pause.

key_provisions.before: Amends the Municipalities Planning Code to give a municipality the option to impose a temporary (reported as up to 18 months per news coverage) moratorium on accepting/considering new applications for high-impact data centers while it revises ordinances and develops conditional-use standards.
key_provisions.after: Pre-introduction memo proposing municipal authority to consider a temporary data-center moratorium; its official page links to SB 1345. The separately retained bill row pa-sb1345 describes the later PN 1889 resolution, maximum term and exceptions. This precursor is not an additional independent bill or an adopted municipal pause.

It does not itself enact a statewide or local moratorium.

Also addresses studies, cost recovery, financial commitments, qualifying co-location and conditional curtailment.

key_provisions.before: Adds Va. Code section 15.2-2209.4. Requires localities to obtain a sound-profile site assessment for new high energy use facilities of 100 MW or more near homes or schools within 500 feet; allows optional review of water, agriculture, parks, historic sites, and forestland.
key_provisions.after: Published chapter/code site-assessment framework requires an applicant's sound assessment before specified local approvals for a new facility reasonably anticipated to require at least 100 MW of retail utility power. Sound impacts concern homes and schools within 500 feet of the facility property boundary; other resource assessments are optional, and utility substation/voltage information is also required subject to stated qualifications. The framework preserves the existing-approval/expansion exception; its phrase “does not exceed an additional 100 megawatts or more” is not converted into a definitive boundary here. The chapter labels the provision 15.2-2209.4; the observed code publishes it as 15.2-2209.5. Later force is not independently confirmed.

key_provisions.before: Would require State Corporation Commission certificates of operation for new high-load facilities exceeding 25 MW, including review of grid sufficiency and customer cross-subsidy risks.
key_provisions.after: Introduced HB155 would require an SCC certificate before operating a facility, or facilities effectively operating together at the Commission's discretion, with electricity demand or contracted capacity exceeding 25 MW and not operating before 2026-07-01. Certification follows applicable notice and hearing and requires specified findings on rates, reliability, utility compliance, clean-energy policy and public interest; review includes grid capacity, environmental and public-health impacts and cross-subsidy. An adequate showing of specified contracts or other measures designed to offset system peak demand creates presumptions on certain findings, not an exemption from the certificate requirement.

status.before: Prefiled 2026-01-06; referred to House Labor and Commerce; subcommittee recommended laying on the table (9-Y 0-N) 2026-02-10; Left in Labor and Commerce (and Education) 2026-02-18 - bill died in House committee.
status.after: Prefiled 2026-01-06; referred to House Labor and Commerce; subcommittee recommended laying on the table (9-Y 0-N) 2026-02-10; left in Labor and Commerce 2026-02-18; official retained page labels the bill failed.

key_provisions.before: Required a high energy use facility site assessment before rezoning, special exception, or special use permit approvals, with mandatory noise review within 500 feet and optional review of water, agriculture, parks, historic, and forest impacts.
key_provisions.after: Enrolled HB1601 would require a locality, before approval of specified zoning applications for a new high energy use facility, to require the applicant to assess its sound profile on residential units and schools within 500 feet of the property boundary, to the extent practicable and within the statutory timeline. A facility qualifies when the applicant reasonably anticipates at application that it will require 100 MW or more of retail utility power. The locality may require specified resource assessments on the site or immediately contiguous land, and must require qualified utility substation and transmission information. The existing-approval expansion or modification exception states that the expansion 'does not exceed an additional 100 megawatts or more'; its numeric boundary is unresolved. Existing local zoning authority is preserved. The enrolled print has blank chapter and approval fields; later post-veto proceedings remain unverified.

Subsequent veto proceedings were not independently established.

key_provisions.before: Would allow local site assessments before data center siting approvals; House-passed version focused on water use and carbon emissions.
key_provisions.after: The engrossed House print would allow a locality, before any approval for siting a data center, to assess the effect on water usage and carbon emissions within the locality. Its House amendments strike the mandatory 'shall' and agricultural-resources language and insert 'may'.

key_provisions.before: Requires registered water users that provide offsite water to report potable and reclaimed water volumes supplied to data centers with DEQ air permits, along with other use categories where available.
key_provisions.after: Published water-reporting act requires covered registered offsite suppliers to report potable and reclaimed water separately for qualifying air-permitted data centers. Other use categories are required to the extent available without utility billing-system modifications; quarterly volumes may substitute where monthly data are unavailable. The act expressly becomes effective 2027-01-01; enactment does not establish that it was already operative at the observation date.

key_provisions.before: Would prevent utility costs substantially related to serving data center customers of 100 MW or more from being recovered from non-data-center customers unless rates substantially recover those costs from data centers.
key_provisions.after: Introduced HB503 would bar inclusion in SCC-approved rates or charges under § 56-585.1 or § 56-585.8 of Phase I or Phase II utility costs, including increased fuel, generation and transmission costs, that are substantially related to electric service to data center customers and would not have been incurred but for their demand, unless the rates or charges are designed to recover, or substantially recover, those costs solely from data center customers. For this provision, a data center customer is a data center under § 58.1-3506(A)(43) with peak demand of 100 MW or greater.

key_provisions.after: Introduced proposal addressing specified localities' data-center zoning, including industrial designation, residential impacts and mitigation measures; incorporated into HB 153. Incorporation does not establish enactment of every introduced HB 511 provision.

key_provisions.before: Senate companion to HB1601.
key_provisions.after: Enrolled SB1449 would require a locality, before approval of specified zoning applications for a new high energy use facility, to require the applicant to assess its sound profile on residential units and schools within 500 feet of the property boundary, to the extent practicable and within the statutory timeline. A facility qualifies when the applicant reasonably anticipates at application that it will require 100 MW or more of retail utility power. The locality may require specified resource assessments on the site or immediately contiguous land, and must require qualified utility substation and transmission information. The existing-approval expansion or modification exception states that the expansion 'does not exceed an additional 100 megawatts or more'; its numeric boundary is unresolved. Existing local zoning authority is preserved. The enrolled print has blank chapter and approval fields; later post-veto proceedings remain unverified.

key_provisions.before: Senate version of high-load certificate legislation; passed Senate with a 90 MW threshold before failing.
key_provisions.after: Senate-passed proposal concerns high-load facilities over 90 MW that were not operating before 2027-01-01, with electric-service/cost conditions. The offered House subcommittee substitute is a separate version and is not treated as adopted Senate text. The bill did not independently enact the proposed requirements.

key_provisions.before: Companion / identical enacted high energy use facility site-assessment bill; incorporated SB130.
key_provisions.after: Observed code site-assessment framework requires an applicant's sound assessment before specified local approvals for a new facility reasonably anticipated to require at least 100 MW of retail utility power. Sound impacts concern homes and schools within 500 feet of the facility property boundary; other resource assessments are optional, and utility substation/voltage information is also required subject to stated qualifications. The framework preserves the existing-approval/expansion exception; its phrase “does not exceed an additional 100 megawatts or more” is not converted into a definitive boundary here. The observed code publishes the framework as 15.2-2209.5 and cites chapters 567 and 568. SB94's own chapter 568 print was not recovered in the inspected cohort; its printed section number remains unverified. Later force is not independently confirmed.
